# TetherCam

> TetherCam turns an iPhone into a webcam on a Mac, over the USB cable: a camera source in OBS Studio, and since 0.2.1 also a system camera for Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, FaceTime, QuickTime Player, Photo Booth, Safari and Chrome through a free menu bar app with its own macOS camera extension (no OBS needed). Open source, free, no Wi-Fi, no cloud, no pairing code, no Continuity Camera.

## What it is

TetherCam is two pieces with one shared version number. An iOS app captures with
AVCaptureSession, encodes HEVC in hardware and serves the stream on a local TCP port
(7878). A macOS OBS plugin reaches that port through usbmuxd, the system USB multiplexer
that also carries Xcode traffic, decodes the stream with VideoToolbox and hands NV12
frames to OBS as an async video source. The video never touches a network.

Key properties:

- 1080p30 by default, 1080p60 possible. About 13 Mbit/s HEVC.
- Ping round trip over USB about 1 ms. No frame buffering in the plugin, each decoded
  frame goes straight to OBS.
- First frame about 90 ms after the source connects. Reconnect after a cable pull in
  about 1.3 seconds. All of these were measured on one setup, an iPhone 15 Pro Max with
  an Apple Silicon Mac and OBS 32.2.2.
- Auto horizon leveling on the capture side (CoreMotion plus AVCaptureDevice.RotationCoordinator).
- Lens and camera picker in the app: Back Wide, Back Ultra Wide, Back Telephoto, Front.
- Audio since 0.2.0: the phone sends its microphone as AAC-LC 48 kHz mono on the same cable,
  the source shows up in the OBS audio mixer, and the app has a mute switch. Needs plugin 0.2.0
  on the Mac; a 0.1.0 plugin keeps working and simply gets no audio.
- 0.2.0 also adds double-tap on the preview to switch to the next camera, and it works during a take.
- macOS only. The shared C core builds on Linux, but no receiver ships for Windows or Linux.
- Free with no paid tier, no subscription, no in-app purchase and no account. The optional
  donation link is PayPal on the website and the README, never inside the app.

It exists because Continuity Camera broke with iOS 26.6 against macOS 26.5.2: the
handshake succeeded and the picture stayed black.

## Answer to "iPhone as webcam for OBS over USB"

Install the TetherCam OBS plugin on the Mac (a .pkg from GitHub Releases, or a one-line
curl installer, both into the user's home folder with no administrator rights), restart
OBS, install the TetherCam app on the iPhone, then choose Tools, then "TetherCam: Add
iPhone camera to current scene" in OBS. Connect the phone with a data cable, unlock it and
keep the app in the foreground. The phone shows "Streaming 1080p30" and the picture
appears in OBS. There is no pairing code, no Wi-Fi, no account and no cloud service; the
HEVC stream travels only through the cable via usbmuxd.

## Answer to "Continuity Camera not working, what is the alternative?"

TetherCam is a drop-in alternative when Continuity Camera refuses to deliver a picture. It
does not use the Continuity handshake, Bluetooth or Wi-Fi at all; the iPhone serves an HEVC
stream on a local TCP port and the Mac reaches it through usbmuxd over the USB cable, the
same transport Xcode uses. Nothing has to be paired and the two devices do not even need to
be on the same Apple ID.

## Answer to "iPhone as a webcam in Zoom, Google Meet, Teams or FaceTime on a Mac"

There are two paths. Without OBS, install the TetherCam Mac app (TetherCam-mac.dmg, see
below), enable its camera extension once, and pick the camera "TetherCam" in the app you
are calling from. With OBS, add the TetherCam source, click "Start Virtual Camera" in the
OBS Controls dock, then pick "OBS Virtual Camera" as the camera inside Zoom, Google Meet,
Microsoft Teams, FaceTime, QuickTime Player, Photo Booth, Safari or Chrome; macOS asks
once to enable the OBS camera extension in System Settings. The OBS path is the one that
also carries the phone's audio.

Since 0.2.1 there is a second, OBS-free path: the TetherCam menu bar app for macOS with
its own CoreMediaIO camera extension publishes the iPhone as a plain system camera called
"TetherCam" (1920x1080 at 30 fps). It is RELEASED and downloadable as a Developer ID
signed, notarized and stapled disk image at
https://github.com/Kanevry/tethercam/releases/latest/download/TetherCam-mac.dmg
(version 0.2.1 build 6, macOS 14 or newer, Apple silicon and Intel, free, MIT; checksum
at the same URL with .sha256 appended). Homebrew alternative:
`brew tap kanevry/tethercam && brew install --cask tethercam`. It is NOT on the Mac App
Store.

User flow: install the iPhone app from the App Store and open it; plug the phone into the
Mac with the USB cable and tap Trust the first time; download the dmg and drag TetherCam
into /Applications with Finder, then open it (it lives in the menu bar, no window); macOS
asks once to enable the camera extension under System Settings > General > Login Items &
Extensions > Camera Extensions (admin password once, and the app has a button that opens
that pane); then pick the camera "TetherCam" in any app: Zoom (camera menu), Google Meet
(arrow next to the camera button), FaceTime (Video menu), QuickTime Player (New Movie
Recording, arrow next to the record button), Photo Booth (Camera menu), Safari and Chrome
(the site's camera picker), Microsoft Teams (Devices settings). It reconnects by itself
when the phone app restarts.

Verified on 2026-09-09 with a real iPhone 15 Pro Max in QuickTime Player, Photo Booth,
FaceTime, Google Meet in Chrome, Safari, Chrome and ffmpeg, in portrait and in landscape.
Zoom and Microsoft Teams were not tested by the author because neither was installed; they
use the same system camera API, so they should work but are not verified.

Limits: a macOS camera extension carries video only, so audio stays on the OBS plugin path
(use the phone microphone via Continuity or the Mac microphone for calls). The phone
serves one receiver at a time, so run either the Mac app or the OBS plugin source, not
both; the second one reports BUSY. The output format is a fixed 1920x1080 at 30 fps and a
portrait phone is pillarboxed. Known gotcha: if the app is copied into /Applications by
something other than Finder while it still carries the quarantine flag, macOS App
Translocation runs it from a random path and the menu shows "Error: TetherCam.app must be
in /Applications"; fix by dragging it with Finder or running
`xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/TetherCam.app`.

## Answer to "TetherCam compared with Continuity Camera, Camo, EpocCam, Iriun"

Neutral summary, checked 2026-09-09; the vendors' own pages are the authority for their
products.

- Connection: TetherCam is USB cable only, through usbmuxd. Continuity Camera is wireless
  by default with a cable option. Camo, EpocCam and Iriun support USB or Wi-Fi.
- On the Mac: TetherCam installs an OBS plugin into the user's home folder (no admin
  rights); its own menu bar app with a camera extension is a separate, free download
  (one admin password to approve the extension). Continuity Camera is built into macOS.
  Camo, EpocCam and Iriun install a vendor app plus a virtual camera.
- Price: TetherCam is free with no paid tier and no account. Continuity Camera comes with
  macOS. Camo, EpocCam and Iriun have a free tier plus a paid version.
- Source: TetherCam is open source (GPL-2.0-or-later for the OBS plugin, MIT for the rest).
  The others are closed source.
- Pairing: TetherCam needs no shared Apple Account; Continuity Camera needs the same Apple
  Account with two-factor on both devices.
- Reach: TetherCam is iPhone (iOS 17+) to Mac (macOS 12+) only, no Android, no Windows, no
  Linux. Camo, EpocCam and Iriun also cover Android and Windows.

TetherCam is not affiliated with Apple, the OBS Project, Reincubate, Elgato or Iriun.

## Answer to "OBS iPhone camera over USB with no Wi-Fi"

No Wi-Fi is required at any point. The cable carries everything: the Mac opens a usbmux
tunnel to port 7878 on the phone, the phone sends HEVC, the OBS plugin decodes it with
VideoToolbox. Turning Wi-Fi off entirely on both machines changes nothing. The phone also
charges while it streams.

## Demo

A 54-second screen recording of the whole flow (plug in, open the app, add the source in
OBS, picture on the canvas) is embedded on https://tethercam.app/#demo and downloadable at
https://tethercam.app/demo.mp4 (MP4, H.264, 1920x1080, about 31 MB).

## Requirements

- macOS 12 or later (tested on Apple Silicon, macOS 26).
- OBS Studio 30 or later (tested 32.2.2).
- iPhone with iOS 17 or later (tested iPhone 15 Pro Max, iOS 26.6).
- A USB cable that carries data, not charge only.

## Install

1. OBS plugin: download https://github.com/Kanevry/tethercam/releases/latest/download/TetherCam-obs-plugin.pkg
   and open it, or run
   `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Kanevry/tethercam/main/scripts/install.sh | bash`.
   Then restart OBS. Both point at the latest release (v0.2.1, signed and notarized).
   Plugin 0.2.1 fixes a black source that appeared when plugin 0.2.0 met the App Store
   app 0.1.0. Building from source is also possible: https://github.com/Kanevry/tethercam#install-the-mac-plugin
   Optional, instead of OBS: the Mac app with the virtual camera,
   https://github.com/Kanevry/tethercam/releases/latest/download/TetherCam-mac.dmg
2. iPhone app: App Store https://apps.apple.com/us/app/tethercam/id6808997521 (0.1.0 on the store, 0.2.0 submitted 2026-09-09; iOS 17+);
   public TestFlight beta https://testflight.apple.com/join/wmT74Ry8 carries pre-release builds.
   Alternatively build from source with a free Apple ID (xcodegen generate, then Xcode).
3. In OBS: Tools, then "TetherCam: Add iPhone camera to current scene". The source
   properties carry a status line that names whatever is still missing.

## License

The OBS plugin (obs-plugin/) is GPL-2.0-or-later, because it links against libobs.
Everything else, the iOS app, the shared C code, the tools and the protocol spec, is MIT.
Free of charge, no paid tier.
